title: Dementia in Down syndrome
blurb: Explain why Alzheimer's disease comes earlier in Down syndrome, use a baseline to spot decline, and rule out treatable mimics first.
question: Nadia, 49, has Down syndrome. Over six months she has started needing prompts to dress, has stopped going to her art group and seems slower to answer. Staff ask whether this is dementia. What should the nurse check first, and what would help measure the change?

teach.body: Chromosome 21 carries the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene. People with Down syndrome have three copies, so they make more amyloid. Alzheimer's changes in the brain (plaques and tangles) are present in virtually all adults with Down syndrome by about 40, and the lifetime risk of Alzheimer's dementia is estimated at 90% or more. In plain English: dementia is far more likely, and much younger, than in the general population, so staff must watch for it from early adulthood.
teach.cite: Nature Reviews Neurology 2019; NHS.uk Down's syndrome

teach.body: NICE NG54 recommends a baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour for all adults with Down's syndrome, so later loss of skills can be measured against the person's own starting point. At annual health checks, ask about any change in behaviour, loss of skills (including self-care) or needing more prompting in recent months. NHS.uk advises regular check-ups from age 30. NG96 asks staff to explain the link with dementia early to people with Down syndrome and their families.

children.sub: Specialist, with DLD, DSDS or DSQIID

teach.text: Do not label every decline 'dementia' because the person has Down syndrome. Hypothyroidism (tested yearly for life), hearing and sight loss, depression and pain are common, treatable and can look exactly like early dementia. Diagnostic overshadowing works both ways: missing dementia, or missing what mimics it.

teach.body: Standard dementia screening tests assume typical education and language, so they are misleading here. NICE NG54 1.7.12 suggests supplementing assessment with measures designed for people with learning disabilities: the Dementia Questionnaire for People with Learning Disabilities (DLD), the Dementia Scale for Down Syndrome (DSDS) or the Dementia Screening Questionnaire for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (DSQIID). Information from carers who know the person well is central (NG54 1.7.5).

The learning disability nurse compares Nadia's current skills with the adaptive behaviour baseline recorded at 25: she now needs prompting for tasks she once did alone. Before suggesting dementia, she asks the GP for thyroid function tests and arranges hearing and eye checks, and screens for low mood after a recent move. Her thyroid result is normal and her hearing is unchanged, so a referral for specialist dementia assessment follows, with staff completing the DSQIID. Nadia is told what is happening in an easy read format.

items: Extra APP gene on chromosome 21 drives early Alzheimer's disease.
NG54 1.7.13: baseline of adaptive behaviour for all adults with Down's syndrome.
Ask about behaviour change, skill loss and more prompting at annual checks (NG54 1.5.4).
Exclude hypothyroidism, sensory loss, depression and pain before diagnosing dementia.
New seizures in later life can signal Alzheimer's disease in Down syndrome.

summary: You can now explain why Alzheimer's disease is common and early in Down syndrome and use a baseline of adaptive behaviour to measure decline. You can rule out treatable mimics such as hypothyroidism, sensory loss and depression before supporting a specialist dementia assessment.

A.q: A carer asks why Alzheimer's disease is so much more common in people with Down syndrome. Which explanation is accurate?
options: An extra copy of the APP gene increases amyloid in the brain
Long-term thyroid treatment damages memory pathways over time
Congenital heart disease reduces blood flow to the brain
Lower physical activity in adulthood leads to brain atrophy
A.why: Chromosome 21 carries the APP gene; three copies increase amyloid production and Alzheimer's pathology, near universal by about age 40.

whyNot.1: Thyroid treatment corrects hypothyroidism; untreated hypothyroidism mimics dementia, but treatment does not cause it.
whyNot.2: Heart disease is common in Down syndrome but is not the reason for Alzheimer's disease.
whyNot.3: Activity matters for general health but is not the genetic mechanism.

A.q: Ben, 25, has Down syndrome and is attending his annual health check. Which assessment does NICE NG54 recommend to help detect dementia in future?
options: A memory test repeated every six months from now on
A brain scan to look for early amyloid changes
A baseline assessment of his adaptive behaviour
A genetic test to confirm the type of trisomy 21
A.why: NG54 1.7.13: complete a baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour with all adults with Down's syndrome so later change can be measured against it.

whyNot.0: NICE does not set six-monthly memory testing; the baseline of adaptive behaviour is the key step.
whyNot.1: Routine brain scanning in a well young adult is not recommended.
whyNot.3: The type of trisomy does not provide a baseline for later decline.

A.q: At the annual health check of Ella, 38, who has Down syndrome, which question does NICE NG54 specifically suggest asking?
options: Whether she has had any falls in the past year
Whether she now needs more prompting in daily tasks
Whether she has any close family history of dementia
Whether she has gained weight in recent months
A.why: NG54 1.5.4: for adults with Down's syndrome ask about any change in behaviour, loss of skills including self-care, or a need for more prompting in recent months.

whyNot.0: Falls matter, but NG54 1.5.4 focuses on behaviour, skills and prompting.
whyNot.2: Her risk is driven by Down syndrome itself, not family history.
whyNot.3: Weight is part of a general check, not the dementia question NICE names.

B.q: Nadia, 49, has Down syndrome. Over six months she needs prompts to dress and has dropped her art group. Which tests should be arranged first?
options: CT head scan and a sleep-deprived EEG
Full blood count and vitamin D
Lung function and an ECG
Thyroid function, hearing and vision
B.why: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and mimics dementia; hearing and vision loss also cause apparent decline. These treatable causes are checked before a dementia diagnosis.

whyNot.0: Imaging and EEG may form part of later specialist assessment but do not exclude the common treatable mimics.
whyNot.1: These are not the priority mimics in this group.
whyNot.2: Nothing suggests a heart or lung cause for skill loss.

B.q: Amira, 46, has Down syndrome. Staff report she has lost interest in activities, is tearful and wakes early. Her thyroid tests are normal. Which condition should be assessed before dementia is assumed?
options: Depression
Delirium
Psychotic illness
Epilepsy
B.why: Tearfulness, loss of interest and early waking suggest depression, which can mimic early dementia and is treatable. NG54 asks for a full assessment of mental health.

whyNot.1: Delirium is acute and fluctuating, often with altered alertness, not a gradual mood change.

B.q: Joseph, 55, has Down syndrome and suspected dementia. A community nurse wants a structured tool to track change over time. Which tool fits NICE NG54?
options: The Mini-Mental State Examination
The DSQIID screening questionnaire
The 4AT rapid delirium screening test
The Abbreviated Mental Test score
B.why: NG54 1.7.12 suggests measures designed for people with learning disabilities, such as the DLD, DSDS and DSQIID.

whyNot.0: The MMSE assumes typical education and language and is unreliable in learning disability.
whyNot.2: The 4AT screens for delirium, not progressive dementia.
whyNot.3: The AMT is a general screening test not designed for people with learning disabilities.

C.q: Michael, 52, has Down syndrome and no history of epilepsy. He has two tonic-clonic seizures in a month, and his carers say he has needed more help with self-care this year. What do these findings most suggest?
options: A side effect of a recent increase in his thyroid dose
A new primary epilepsy unrelated to his other changes
Late-onset epilepsy linked to Alzheimer's disease
Seizures caused by low mood and poor sleep at night
C.why: In Down syndrome, new seizures in later life are closely linked to the emergence of Alzheimer's disease (late-onset myoclonic epilepsy in Down syndrome). With skill loss, dementia assessment is needed.

whyNot.0: Nothing indicates a dose change, and correct thyroid treatment does not explain skill loss.
whyNot.1: Combined with skill loss, the seizures are likely linked to Alzheimer's disease, not unrelated.
whyNot.3: Poor sleep can lower the seizure threshold, but low mood and sleep do not explain first seizures at 52 together with loss of self-care skills.

C.q: Peter, 52, has Down syndrome and Alzheimer's dementia. He lives in a shared house and has started leaving at night. Staff want to lock the front door. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Lock the door at night because it keeps Peter safe from harm
Ask his brother to sign consent for the locked door
Increase his evening sedation to help him sleep through
Assess his capacity and consider less restrictive options
C.why: Locking Peter in is a significant restriction. Under the MCA 2005 his capacity for this decision is assessed; if he lacks it, any decision is in his best interests and the less restrictive option is considered, with lawful authorisation if it amounts to a deprivation of liberty.

whyNot.0: Safety does not remove the need for a lawful, least restrictive decision.
whyNot.1: Being his brother gives no power to consent for Peter; even an attorney or deputy decides in his best interests and cannot authorise a deprivation of liberty.
whyNot.2: Sedation for staff convenience is a chemical restraint and not the least restrictive option.

C.q: Lucy, 21, has Down syndrome. Her parents ask when they should talk with her about the link between Down syndrome and dementia. What does NICE advise?
options: Explain early and accessibly to Lucy and her family
Wait until she is 40, when brain changes are common
Wait until any signs of memory problems first appear
Tell her parents and leave it to them to tell Lucy
C.why: NG96 1.5.36: explain early to people with learning disabilities, particularly Down's syndrome, and their families about the link with dementia, using accessible information.

whyNot.1: Waiting until 40 delays planning, including the baseline assessment recommended for all adults.
whyNot.2: Waiting for symptoms removes the chance to plan while Lucy can fully take part.
whyNot.3: Lucy has the right to accessible information herself; NICE names the person and the family.

reteach.title: Measure against the person, not the population
reteach.question: Why can a carer's notes from when the person was 25 be more useful than any memory test?

blocks.body: People with Down syndrome have varied abilities, so there is no 'normal score'. A baseline of the person's own adaptive behaviour (self-care, routines, skills) recorded in early adulthood is the ruler against which later loss is measured. Without it, decline is guessed rather than shown.

blocks.text: Thyroid, hearing, vision, mood and pain come first. A treatable cause found is a life changed; a dementia label wrongly given closes doors.

explain.body: Three copies of the APP gene on chromosome 21 raise amyloid levels. Alzheimer's brain changes are near universal by about 40 and lifetime risk of dementia is 90% or more.

test.q: Which gene on chromosome 21 links Down syndrome with early Alzheimer's disease?
options: MECP2
FMR1
UBE3A
APP
test.why: The amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene is on chromosome 21.

whyNot.0: MECP2 is linked to Rett syndrome.
whyNot.1: FMR1 is the fragile X gene.
whyNot.2: UBE3A is linked to Angelman syndrome on chromosome 15.

explain.body: NG54 1.7.13: baseline of adaptive behaviour for all adults with Down's syndrome. NG54 1.5.4: at annual health checks ask about changes in behaviour, loss of skills, or needing more prompting.

test.q: What should a baseline assessment for an adult with Down syndrome mainly record?
options: The person's IQ score on a standard test
The person's usual adaptive behaviour and skills
The person's family history of early dementia
The person's amyloid level on a baseline brain scan
test.why: NG54 1.7.13 specifies a baseline assessment of adaptive behaviour, which shows later skill loss.

whyNot.0: IQ alone does not capture everyday skills and is not what NICE specifies.
whyNot.2: Family history does not provide a personal baseline.
whyNot.3: Scanning is not part of the recommended baseline.

explain.body: Hypothyroidism, hearing loss, sight loss, depression, pain and life events can all look like dementia. Thyroid function is tested yearly for life in Down syndrome.

test.q: A woman with Down syndrome is slower and more forgetful. Which blood test is most important before considering dementia?
options: Liver function
Thyroid function
Serum calcium level
Blood glucose
test.why: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome, rises with age and can mimic dementia and depression.

whyNot.0: Liver function is not the key mimic in this group.
whyNot.2: Calcium is not the priority test here.
whyNot.3: Glucose matters generally but hypothyroidism is the classic mimic.

explain.body: NG54 1.7.12: supplement dementia assessment with DLD, DSDS or DSQIID. NG54 1.7.5: use carers' information about behaviour change.

test.q: Who provides the most important information when assessing possible dementia in a man with Down syndrome?
options: The consultant from a single clinic visit
The GP from his medical records alone
Carers who know his usual skills well
The pharmacist from his medication list
test.why: NG54 1.7.5: use information from carers about changes in behaviour; they know his baseline.

whyNot.0: One visit cannot show change over time.
whyNot.3: Medicines are reviewed, but they do not show skill change.
